Overviews
passage-en-00118

Yet he also studied under Mohsen Fayz, Mollâ Sadrâ’s son-in-law and most brilliant pupil. The result was that Qâzî Sa’îd’s sacred philosophy eventually met Mollâ Sadrâ’s in the region of the mundus imaginalis. In his account of being, however, Qâzî Sa’îd insists on a radical distinction: the word “being” has wholly different meanings when applied to the Principle of being and to beings themselves.
Overviews
passage-en-00119

The Principle remains, in its very essence, beyond the being of which it is the source; created beings, by contrast, belong essentially to the order of creation. According to the teaching of the Shiite Imams themselves, only the via negationis—negative, or apophatic, theology, which approaches God by saying what cannot be said of God—allows us even to approach the Principle from afar.
Overviews
passage-en-00120

All the more necessary, then, is the primordial theophany, the original manifestation of the divine: the metaphysical pleroma of the “Fourteen beings of light.” They are the bearers of the divine Names and Attributes with which affirmative theology is concerned. On all these points, Qâzî Sa’îd Qommî stands close to the teaching of the Absconditum, the utterly hidden divine reality, found in both Ismaili gnosis and the Shaykhi School (see Book VI below).
Overviews
passage-en-00121

His commentary on a text deeply studied by the philosophers of Imamite Shiism, the Story of the White Cloud, reads it as a narrative of spiritual initiation. It also allows him to return to his own theory of space and time, for that theory makes it possible to understand events that, while not historical in the ordinary sense, are by no means merely mythical. Here again, the philosophers of the School of Isfahan have something to contribute to debates of our own time.
Overviews
en-overview-5
Overview of Book VI
Overviews
passage-en-00122

Book VI is devoted to the Shaykhi School, or “Shaykhism.” The school, whose center at the time of writing was in Kerman in southeastern Iran, did not choose this name for itself. Others gave it to the disciples of Shaykh AHMAD AHSÂ’Î (1826), who was simply known as the Shaykh, so powerful was the impression of his personality on followers and opponents alike.
Overviews
passage-en-00123

Several reasons justify giving this school such a prominent place here. Its spiritual teachers were figures of exceptional stature. They produced an immense body of writings, many still in manuscript, marked throughout by a determination to preserve and deepen, in complete fidelity, the whole teaching of the Shiite Imams on divine wisdom and mystical knowledge. Inevitably, their renewal of themes that many Shiites had forgotten appeared to the ill-informed or ill-disposed as a dangerous innovation.
Overviews
passage-en-00124

Hence the painful history of the Shaykhi School, one of the episodes in which Imamite Shiism struggled against itself. For Iranian thought, and for the history of spiritual knowledge more generally, this was an especially dramatic moment.
Overviews
passage-en-00125

In seeking to preserve and deepen the full inner teaching of the holy Imams—the whole of Imamite gnosis—the Shaykhi masters were led to develop points of doctrine that could be understood only by minds with a particular gift for metaphysics and sacred philosophy. They therefore had to contend with hostile critics who read them without understanding them, or who had neither read nor understood them. Equally troublesome were certain overzealous disciples and admirers who understood no better. This book gives the biographies of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsâ’î and his successors, with enough bibliographical information to suggest the extraordinary scale of their work.
Overviews
passage-en-00126

Some have conceded that Shaykh Ahmad Ahsâ’î was a “man of God” of outstanding devotion, while claiming that he never really understood metaphysical questions or the language of philosophers. The pages devoted here to his cosmology and his account of the origin of the human being are enough to refute such superficial and unfounded judgments. Particular attention is paid to the doctrine known as the “fourth pillar.” It has provoked some of the worst misunderstandings and controversies, precisely because it is among the hardest teachings to grasp.
Overviews
passage-en-00127

Yet it expresses a fundamental and traditional aspect of Shiite esotericism: by keeping those who bear this spiritual responsibility unknown, it protects the perspective of the final things, and with it the meaning and future mission of the tradition.
Overviews
en-overview-6
Overview of Book VII
Overviews
passage-en-00128

Book VII brings together the essential features of this vision of the final things, centered on the person of the Twelfth Imam, the “Imam hidden from the senses but present in the hearts of his faithful.” He is a compelling figure, endowed with all the power of a primordial Image. This Image governs the hidden possibilities within Shiite consciousness, so that what lies concealed there, yet is always on the verge of appearing, can at last become visible. For more than ten centuries, the sacred biography of the Twelfth Imam and the accounts of his manifestations have formed the very history of Shiite consciousness.
Overviews
passage-en-00129

More precisely, they form a sacred history: their events take place on the level of visionary experience. As we have repeatedly emphasized, such events are not history in the ordinary sense, but they are even less to be dismissed as myth. This sacred biography begins with the Twelfth Imam’s birth. The account of the mystical betrothal of his mother, the Byzantine princess Narkès, to the Eleventh Imam reveals an attention to Christianity expressed nowhere else in Islam in quite this way. It suggests the possibility of an “esoteric ecumenism,” a spiritual kinship reaching across religious boundaries.
Overviews
passage-en-00130

With the Twelfth Imam the “pleroma of the Twelve Imams” is complete. If the Prophet is included in the count, the Twelfth Imam is the thirteenth of the Fourteen Immaculate Ones. Present to both past and future, he is the Seal of the cycle of spiritual initiation that follows the cycle of prophecy. He is therefore also the Seal of prophetic philosophy and of the Shiite understanding of sacred history.
Overviews
passage-en-00131

The present age of his “occultation” (ghaybat), his concealment from outward sight, is a time “between times.” It will last until his final appearing—the parousia—brings our aeon to completion. This very concealment protects spiritual realities from being reduced to social institutions or material things. The person and role of the Twelfth Imam correspond strikingly to the Zoroastrian Persian idea of the final Savior or transfigurer, the Saoshyant. Zoroastrian ethics, it has been said, takes the form of something like an order of chivalry. In a similar way, an ideal of spiritual chivalry grew up around the Twelfth Imam.
Overviews
passage-en-00132

On one side it connects the moral and spiritual character of ancient Zoroastrian Iran with that of Shiite Iran. On the other, it establishes a link between the spiritual chivalry of Islamic Iran and that of the West, an idea already proclaimed in the West during the twelfth century. Certain Shiite thinkers—for example, a pupil of Mîr Dâmâd—explicitly identify the Twelfth Imam with the Zoroastrian Resurrector. A Shiite tradition likewise identifies him with the Paraclete promised in the Gospel of John. These correspondences govern the whole of Book VII, in which the author seeks to bring their hidden implications to light.
Overviews
passage-en-00133

Several texts translated here for the first time show what Shiite consciousness understands by this spiritual chivalry—javânmardî in Persian, fotowwat in Arabic. It cannot be separated from the idea of the cycle of prophecy or from the “Friends of God”: those who participate in walâyat, the inward spiritual reality of prophecy. That is why the authors studied here trace the distant origins of this chivalry to Seth, the son and “Imam” of Adam, in whom it is identified with the very idea of Sufism (tasawwof). Abraham, the father of the knights of faith, is said to have separated fotowwat from tasawwof at the request of his followers. In this way, fotowwat spread through the ideal of fellowship, until every craft and occupation could become an act of chivalrous service.
Overviews
passage-en-00134

Some shared names and patterns might at first seem unimportant. Yet the working of primordial Images reveals them to be full of meaning, quite apart from any demonstrable chain of historical influence.
Overviews
passage-en-00135

Consider the Green Island, the pleroma of the Twelve, and the concealment of the “thirteenth.” Their images and structures reappear among fourteenth-century “Friends of God”—the Johannite knights of the Green Island at Strasbourg—as well as among the twelve (or thirteen) knights in a famous unfinished poem by Goethe. The very recurrence of the name “Friends of God” is striking. It is given to people whose ideal and way of life belong neither to the clergy nor to the laity, but precisely to the spiritual knight. This was also the ideal proposed in the twelfth century by Wolfram von Eschenbach, who forcefully proclaimed the idea of a chivalry shared by West and East, Christianity and Islam.
Overviews
passage-en-00136

Book II already explored the convergences between Parsifal’s Quest for the Grail and the Iranian epic, between prophetic philosophy and the mystical epic. Once again, then, we must ask: where does the philosopher stand? These thinkers affirmed that philosopher and prophet share a common calling, and they understood the prophets’ mission as one of spiritual chivalry. For them, therefore, the philosopher’s service is also a divine service—an idea that certain Jewish Kabbalists have expressed with particular excellence. Something like a spiritual chivalry thus arises wherever we encounter the “phenomenon of the Holy Book.” It is an Abrahamic chivalry, because Abraham is its father and because it bears walâyat: the inner spiritual dimension of all three branches of the Abrahamic tradition.
Overviews
passage-en-00137

Just as the Twelfth Imam is the Seal of the “Friends of God” and the Seal of spiritual chivalry, so a Shiite tradition identifies him with the Paraclete of John’s Gospel. Here the philosophers of Imamite Shiism divide sacred history into periods in a way that corresponds to the scheme developed in the twelfth century by Joachim of Fiore, whose influence on Western philosophy continued for centuries. On both sides, this division rests less on chronological time than on an intuition of time as it is spiritually lived; in objective historical time, these periods actually coexist.
Overviews
passage-en-00138

And on both sides, everyone called to the life of a spiritual knight belongs already to the reign of the Spirit, the Paraclete, the walâyat of the Twelfth Imam. Neither tradition awaits the revelation of a new Book. What they await is the spiritual understanding (intelligentia spiritualis, ta’wîl) of everything that has come before. Its living instruments are the “Friends of God,” or Viri spirituales, the spiritual men; it frees human beings from every form of bondage and every hell.
Overviews
passage-en-00139

We return, finally, to a fundamental problem already raised in Book I: the widespread secularization of the West. The reign of the Paraclete originally meant the Church of John replacing the Church of Peter. Later, the idea of the Paraclete’s reign was secularized into a program of social messianism. We have already noted how difficult it is to translate words such as “laicization” and “secularization” accurately into Persian or Arabic. Those words presuppose the existence of the Church as an institution, a phenomenon that has no equivalent in Islam.
Overviews
passage-en-00140

Our social and political ideologies are, in fact, secularized theologies. What they have produced is certainly not the Church of John. Rather, they have produced something like a post-Church of Peter: a form succeeding the Church while retaining its principal features in secularized form. What happens, then, when such ideologies enter traditional societies that lack the theological history these ideologies presuppose? This question concerns metaphysicians no less than sociologists.

1. Mîr Dâmâd and the School of Isfahan
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00143

More than one “passionate pilgrim” has fallen under Isfahan’s spell, losing himself in dreams among its gardens, beneath the shade of its green domes. Art historians and archaeologists have preserved the legacy of the Safavids and kept alive, in the present, the significance of this great city of art in Islamic Iran. André Godard has movingly described the magnificent sight that greets the thoughtful traveler on an autumn evening, as the gentle light begins to fade.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00144

Having climbed the lower slopes of the mountain to the south, the traveler turns to look across an immense valley bordered by deserts. From one side to the other stretches a lake of greenery, out of which rise glazed domes and towers. Isfahan, Godard writes, “isolated amid deserts, secret, wonderfully adorned, and laden with history, is an image of exaltation in solitude more truly even than Toledo or Aranjuez. Perhaps it is impossible to understand fully the art, and the soul, of Iran without knowing the poignant beauty of this city.”
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00145

Indeed. Yet it is into spiritual Isfahan that we wish to enter, to discover something of the hidden lives of those souls whose meditations infused the city and its surrounding landscape, transforming both into a spiritual city and a spiritual landscape bearing the distinctive imprint of Iran. This is not an easy task. Walking beside a colleague who is an archaeologist or art historian, the philosopher, the student of the “divine sciences,” might well feel a certain frustration. He knows that thinkers whose names and some of whose works are familiar to him once lived, meditated, and taught in these gardens, in the exquisite shade of these old colleges.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00146

Yet finding definite traces of their presence is not always easy. At least the traces of Mîr Dâmâd have not vanished. The Sadr madrasa, where he taught, still stands in the heart of the Great Bazaar. Its four sides still enclose a broad, delightful garden planted with trees, along whose paths philosophers and theologians of every age still walk in solemn reflection, as Sadrâ Shîrâzî, Mohsen Fayz, and so many others must once have done. We would need to call to mind, too, the masters who lived and taught in the other colleges, and the generations of attentive students who followed them.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00147

Together they sustained a philosophy and a theology bearing their unmistakable stamp. They carried within themselves the challenge and the hope embodied in Shiism, and drew upon the rich possibilities for philosophical reflection contained in the figure of the Imam. Their lives of study—sometimes secluded, sometimes stirred by fierce debates in which their deepest convictions were at stake—continued until the days of the pensive, weak Shah Soltân Hosayn (1694–1722). Withdrawn into his excessively exquisite little prayer chamber and oblivious to the Afghan threat, he allowed a sudden catastrophe to unfold: the sack of Isfahan, the end of the Safavid dynasty, and the scattering of its libraries.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00148

For more than two centuries, however, a spiritual family of philosophers, theologians, and theosophers had flourished there. Some years ago, we proposed gathering their shared concerns—without overlooking the differences to which we shall return—under the name “School of Isfahan.” This name seems, indeed, to have entered the vocabulary of our Iranian colleagues. To this day, the names and principal works of these thinkers are familiar to every Iranian theologian and every philosopher of the traditional schools. Their influence has remained fruitful from century to century. It was transmitted throughout the Qajar period, and today their works, particularly those of Mollâ Sadrâ Shîrâzî, are helping to inspire a revival of traditional philosophy, precisely because the problems they explored have never ceased to matter.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00149

In the West, by contrast, recognition of this school’s importance has come only in our own time. It is strange that so many European travelers and residents who wrote about Persia in the very period when these thinkers lived had no real contact with the philosophers of Isfahan.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00150

Perhaps one consolation amid the moral disarray of our iron age is that certain spiritual and philosophical conditions now exist—or might be brought into being—that make at least some communication between souls possible. That is why the names and works of the School of Isfahan, whose thinkers lived at the same time as Giordano Bruno and Jacob Boehme, Descartes and Leibniz, now confront us as urgent invitations to encounter them. The “Platonists of Persia” (Ishrâqiyân-e Iran) were contemporaries of the “Cambridge Platonists.”
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00151

We must put an end to the sorry state of affairs in which a comparative history of philosophy leaves its column for the Middle East desperately empty between the great mystic Jâmî (1495) and the Bâb (1850).
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00152

We must also overcome the situation Edward Browne lamented more than thirty years ago, when he complained that the most interesting subject in Shiite theology had “scarcely yet received from European Orientalists the attention it deserves.” The deeper reason for this neglect is no doubt that the task exceeds the technical training of an Orientalist as such. It requires another kind of preparation, and above all an inborn calling: that of the philosopher, the theologian, or, more broadly, the seeker in the ilâhiyât, the “divine sciences”—sciences that the agnosticism of our age no longer knows very well how to distinguish from the “human sciences.”
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00153

Yet philosophers and theologians have rarely abandoned their customary programs to venture into Oriental studies. Even without this deeper obstacle, the neglect would have had its excuses. The sources are not always easy to reach. Many works survive only in manuscript, and manuscripts in private collections can be particularly difficult to locate.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00154

Considerable progress has been made in recent years, with catalogs published for major public collections, but the work is far from complete. Other essential works were published long ago in densely printed lithographic editions, now extremely rare and furnished with neither contents pages nor indexes. The unfortunate researcher enters an enchanted forest where finding his way requires training and an unfailing memory.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00155

Our immediate task, then, is the rediscovery of the sources. It calls for a united effort by philosophers trained in Oriental studies and a new generation of Iranian philosophers, whose responsibility it is to make this spiritual universe present in our time—a universe whose meaning and message have lasting value. For all the complexity of the undertaking, I do not think it unduly optimistic to say that it has begun.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00156

Many pages of the present work have already evoked the School of Isfahan and suggested its defining features. The spiritual types outlined by Sâ'inoddîn Ispahânî (Book IV, Chapter III) gave us an opportunity to recall the difference between the fate of Avicennian philosophy in Iran and its fate in the medieval Latin West. The more closely we study the thinkers of Isfahan, the more striking that contrast becomes. Comparative philosophy thus has an especially fruitful task before it: to bring forward a contrasting witness to the path eventually taken by the West. I say contrasting witness deliberately. This comparison must attempt something much more serious than identifying formal patterns.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00157

Because Avicenna’s works were translated from Arabic into Latin, we can speak of a shared Avicennian moment in East and West during the twelfth and thirteenth centuries. That common element gives us, in itself, a point of reference from which to identify the divergence that then widened from century to century. The decisive comparison will not be based on the different historical and social circumstances of the two worlds, but on the horizon proper to the “divine sciences.” Seen from that horizon, the survival of Avicennian philosophy in Iran and its failure in the West must have a significance that has scarcely yet been examined.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00158

Since the research initiated by Étienne Gilson, we have known that medieval scholasticism and Cartesian philosophy are not wholly unrelated worlds. The dramas that marked the history of medieval scholastic philosophy continued to reverberate—sometimes even to repeat themselves exactly, beneath a different vocabulary—in the most “modern” philosophy. Among these dramas we must count the failure of Latin Avicennianism and its submersion by Averroism.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00159

As we have already suggested, the opposition between Avicenna and Averroes becomes a symbol of the different destinies of two cultures. For a long time, historians supposed that Islamic philosophy disappeared into the sands after Averroes, while Averroism passed into the Latin West and endured there. Latin Averroism continued to be represented in a number of Western universities until the eighteenth century. New commentaries extended Averroes’ thought in the West, while in Iran it was Avicenna’s work that continued, down to our own time, to stimulate successive generations of commentators.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00160

The contrast is striking: the name of Averroes (Ibn Roshd) remained almost unknown in the East. The crises that Averroism was to provoke in Western consciousness had no real counterpart there. While new Western commentaries developed the work of Averroes, Avicenna’s thought grew in Iran, century after century, through new commentaries of its own. Meanwhile, two other names, long unfamiliar in the West, came to exercise an ever greater influence on the philosophy of eastern Islam: Sohrawardî and Mohyiddîn Ibn 'Arabî.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00161

We have already attempted to trace the achievement of Sohrawardî, the young master who, in the twelfth century, “revived the theosophical wisdom of ancient Persia” (Book II). From then on, ancient Iran was no longer merely a store of epic memories and legends for Islamic Persia. Through the interpretive genius of the Shaykh al-Ishrâq, it became a spiritual tradition integrated into Islamic spirituality. As for the vast body of work left by Ibn 'Arabî—perhaps the greatest visionary theosopher of all time—Haydar Âmolî has already shown us how easily Shiite theosophy took it into itself, recognizing in it something of its own inheritance.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00162

There was only one point of disagreement: the question of the Seal of walâyat, the spiritual authority or guardianship that continues the inner meaning of prophecy. Once that issue was settled, nothing stood in the way of Shiite theosophy’s assimilation of Ibn 'Arabî’s work. The Shiite commentaries on the Fosûs, including those of Haydar Âmolî and Sâ'inoddîn Ispahânî, and the great fifteenth-century work of Ibn Abî Jomhûr, bear witness to this. Mollâ Sadrâ’s thought, too, would be deeply shaped by his meditation on Ibn 'Arabî.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00163

At the same time, the traditions (hadith) transmitted from the Shiite Imams—above all the great collections of Kolaynî and Sadûq Ibn Bâbûyeh—became the subject of systematic theosophical commentaries. Those of Mollâ Sadrâ and Qâzî Sa'îd Qommî are monumental works, revealing how powerfully the Imams’ teachings stimulated philosophical meditation. Our thinkers were perfectly aware of this. Unfortunately, the body of traditions attributed to the Imams remained little known, if not entirely unknown, in the West for a very long time.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00164
Thus, when one emphasizes what was, and remains, self-evident to these thinkers, one may be met with discreet, perhaps ironic irritation—as though one had invented the whole thing!
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00165

In short, all these elements taken together—Sohrawardî’s theosophy of Light, Ibn 'Arabî’s mystical gnosis, and the prophetic philosophy and spirituality of walâyat taught by the Imams—give us some sense of the intellectual and spiritual atmosphere in which Iranian Avicennian philosophy lived and flourished, right down to our own day. Avicenna’s own works, of course, continued to be read and commented upon; I have already mentioned the highly individual commentaries of Mollâ Sadrâ and Ahmad 'Alawî, among others.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00166
But these Avicennian thinkers did not remain confined to questions settled once and for all. Their Avicennianism expanded with each new generation.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00167

It is for this reason that we described Iranian Avicennianism as a contrasting witness—a witness able to shed light on the Latin Avicennianism that was so soon defeated in the West, and to disclose the reasons and circumstances of that defeat, together with its consequences. It need only show what its own centuries-long existence in the Iranian world made possible. The conditions and development of what we may call “Illuminationist Avicennianism” and “Shiite Avicennianism” were wholly different from those of the episode in medieval Latin scholasticism known as “Avicennizing Augustinianism.”
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00168

Avicenna’s theory of knowledge, whose central idea and further implications we have had occasion to discuss, could provide the framework for a comparative study that remains to be undertaken. Such a study should ask what analogies or affinities exist between the doctrine of the Active Intelligence among the Latin Averroists and Hegel’s conception of Spirit in his phenomenology. At the very time when a form of philosophical consciousness was being prepared and developed in the West—a form that would culminate in Hegel’s philosophy of historical Spirit, whose interpretations or ruins still weigh upon the recognized problems of Western thought with the burden of their mythology—the philosophers of Isfahan were pursuing Avicenna’s theory of knowledge in an altogether different direction.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00169

Earlier, we emphasized the identification of the Active Intelligence ('Aql fa''âl), the “Angel of Knowledge,” with the Holy Spirit. In the Islamic understanding, this Holy Spirit is identified—returning in this respect to certain Christian conceptions from before the Council of Nicaea—with Gabriel, the “Angel of the Annunciation” sent to Mary (Maryam) and the “Angel of Revelation” who communicates divine revelation to the prophets. This identification immediately places philosophical inquiry within the aims and ultimate purpose of a “prophetic philosophy.” As we noted before, its angelology of knowledge culminates in an Imamology of Knowledge: an understanding of knowledge centered on the spiritual role of the Imams.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00170

Here a philosophy of the Holy Spirit stands opposed to the dialectical philosophy of historical Spirit, of Spirit descending into historical time. It is a prophetic theosophy that leads every history back to metahistory, the order of spiritual meaning beyond ordinary historical events. It finds expression in the idea of the cycle of prophecy and the cycle of walâyat, directed toward the advent of the Twelfth Imam, the “Hidden Imam,” whom some of our authors—Haydar Âmolî, for example—explicitly identify with the Paraclete named in the Gospel tradition, which they also knew. This ordering gives each spiritual individuality a place and a meaning confirmed by Avicenna’s theory of knowledge.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00171

By contrast, a totalitarian dialectic of historical Spirit, whether Averroist or Hegelian in inspiration, destroys that individuality. It also destroys the imaginal world, the realm of real spiritual images and events. Without that world, spiritual events and the facts of sacred history face a false dilemma: if they cannot be fitted into the record of empirical history, they must be dismissed as myth.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00172

Yet in the traditions of the Imams themselves we encountered a principle of interpretation that already outwitted the traps of historicism. Spiritual events do not simply fall “into history.” Their meaning and content transcend the limits and visible circumstances of the historical world to which they are related. But on the level of their own world, they have a time and a “history” of their own.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00173

Hence the fundamental difference between Shiite ta'wîl—the spiritual interpretation practiced by Haydar Âmolî, Mollâ Sadrâ, or Semnânî—and the Averroist ta'wîl that escapes into “allegory.” In the last analysis, the choice is this: either preserve the proper subject matter and meaning of the ilâhiyât, the “divine sciences,” or absorb them into the “human sciences” and nothing more. This is undoubtedly too brief an account to provide all the arguments it requires. Still, it had to be included here as a preliminary outline. For one thing, it helps us locate the School of Isfahan, and with it Iranian philosophy as a whole, in relation to Western philosophy, by suggesting the landmarks of a comparison.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00174

For another, it challenges the distorted conception that had mutilated the very idea of Islamic philosophy by, paradoxically, overlooking its most important province. We have read brilliant syntheses explaining that when the “Arabs” look back beyond Islam into their own past, they find nothing but the desert. Such a claim deserves closer examination in light of what is now known about the antiquities of pre-Islamic Arabia. In any case, when we speak of Iranian philosophy and the School of Isfahan, it is not the “Arabs” who are in question.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00175

We must remember that every Iranian adolescent, studying Ferdawsî’s Shâh-Nâmeh, finds himself not in a desert but in the company of the heroes of the Iranian epic. So, too, does the Iranian philosopher familiar with Sohrawardî’s work. Perhaps it is only because some writers never even suspected the repeated rebirths of philosophy in Iran that they could speak of the hardening and decline of Islamic thought, and blame it on an exclusive, rigid Aristotelianism. It is difficult to speak of intellectual stagnation in the case of Haydar Âmolî, Mîr Dâmâd, Mollâ Sadrâ, Qâzî Sa'îd Qommî, or their pupils. It would be no easier to speak of rigid Aristotelianism among the Ishrâqîyûn, the “Platonists of Persia.” And anyone who has spent time with Avicennian philosophy knows, as Averroes himself knew, how hard it is to find in it Aristotelianism pure and simple, whether rigid or otherwise.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00176

In fact, the judgments just mentioned arise more from sociological surveys of philosophy than from genuinely philosophical investigation. Such swift overviews may give the mind an immediate satisfaction, but they hold many disappointments in store for demanding scholars, who eventually discover that the very tasks capable of opening new vistas were neglected. Those tasks take time. They require us to examine the details and to work patiently into the depths of the thoughts and visions preserved in substantial works that, as we have said, are not always easily accessible.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00177

Above all, the metaphysician must remain within the horizon of the “divine sciences” (ilâhiyât), resisting interpretations that may flatter contemporary tastes but whose first effect is to distort what those sciences are actually concerned with. That is all we wished to suggest in our preliminary approach to the spiritual city of Isfahan.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00178

We could have no better guide into that city than Mîr Dâmâd. He was, in a sense, the leading figure of the School of Isfahan, the intellectual master of several generations of philosophers, even though the works of his brilliant pupils seem in practice to have displaced his own. His name is familiar to anyone in Iran with even a modest education in philosophy and theology. Certain forms of popular devotion revere him almost as a saint.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00179

Yet his reputation seems scarcely to have crossed the borders of the Iranian world in the broad sense: the regions where Persian predominated as a language of learning and culture. Thus manuscripts of Mîr Dâmâd’s works are still numerous in Pakistani libraries but exceedingly rare elsewhere.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00180

The honorific title given to him is revealing in itself. He is called Mo'allim-e thâlîth, the “Third Teacher.” The First Teacher, Magister primus, is understood to be Aristotle—an Aristotle also credited with the celebrated Theology—while the Second Teacher, Magister secundus, was and remains al-Fârâbî, the philosopher who set Avicenna “on the way.” As we may suspect, this title implies a division of the history of philosophy into periods quite unlike the one ordinarily accepted in the West today.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00181

Yet it must fit the theosophy of history, the “prophetic philosophy,” whose outline we recalled above for this very reason. If Iranian consciousness allows some six or seven centuries to pass after al-Fârâbî before recognizing a philosophical event deserving the name “appearance of the Third Teacher,” it is because it perceives in the work that dominates Iranian Shiite Avicennianism something of decisive and exceptional importance. We have just tried to suggest what that something is by tracing the characteristic features of the School of Isfahan.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00182

We can gather those features into a single picture by bringing together the men whose honorific names have made them symbols: Shaykh Sadûq (Ibn Bâbûyeh), the “trustworthy” transmitter of thousands of traditions from the Imams and a pillar of Imamite Shiism; Shaykh al-Ra'îs, Avicenna, the “chief philosopher”; Shaykh al-Ishrâq, Sohrawardî, master of the Light of the East, of cognitio matutina, the knowledge of dawn; Shaykh al-Akbar, Ibn 'Arabî, Doctor maximus, the Greatest Master; and Mo'allim-e thâlîth, Mîr Dâmâd, Magister tertius, the Third Teacher.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00183

There are others, of course, and we have already named several of them. Brilliant as the Safavid Renaissance was, and favorable as the circumstances open to philosophers could be—despite the restrictions Mollâ Sadrâ would experience so painfully—the School of Isfahan did not spring into being from nowhere. Mîr Dâmâd’s own teachers, and the spiritual figures mentioned in the preceding book, remind us of all that made it possible. Nor should the school be treated as a single, undivided body of doctrine. Important differences of detail separate Mîr Dâmâd’s philosophical positions from those of his most famous pupil, Mollâ Sadrâ Shîrâzî, and both from those of Mollâ Rajab 'Alî Tabrîzî and his disciple Qâzî Sa'îd Qommî. These differences are themselves the surest sign of philosophical vitality.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00184

Yet all these thinkers share one defining feature of their spiritual character, one we have already found in Sohrawardî and shall find again in Mîr Dâmâd and his successors. They are philosophers, but also profoundly spiritual men. Their philosophy does not remain merely theoretical—not because they seek what we today call practical results and useful applications, for a philosophy that looked to those things for its justification would already have betrayed its vocation.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00185

For these thinkers, putting philosophy into practice means transforming the philosopher’s entire inner life. It means fostering in themselves, in their students, and in everyone touched by their teaching the perfection of a human type devoted to “divine wisdom”—a type whose necessity and meaning today’s homo oeconomicus, the human being conceived solely in economic terms, may no longer even suspect.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00186

So although Mîr Dâmâd has a reputation as a particularly obscure philosopher, the two ecstatic confessions translated later in this chapter show that he was much more besides. They reveal the secret of his ultimate experience, at the summit of his soul. We remain faithful to his own teaching when we say that he was a complete philosopher because his philosophy led him to ecstatic experience, and a consummate mystic because that experience helped him to articulate a metaphysics of ecstasy. In every respect, this is both the teaching and the practice of Sohrawardî.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00187

Above all, then, we should remember that this philosopher, famous for his difficulty, was also a soul alive with mystical experience. Such a union refutes, by the evidence of lived experience, the crude classifications encouraged by an overly dogmatic psychology of character—classifications that would treat as mutually exclusive the spiritual gifts that an ishrâqî sage is called precisely to unite in himself.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00188

In Sohrawardî’s case, it means opening the Book of Oriental Theosophy with a reform of logic and ending it with a reminder of ecstasy. In Mîr Dâmâd’s, it means being a speculative theologian—but in a sense that recalls the Latin speculum, “mirror”: the soul itself becomes the mirror of its visions, and when it discovers this, self-knowledge culminates in mystical experience. For his own pen name (takhallos), Mîr Dâmâd chose the word that most perfectly expresses Sohrawardî’s philosophy: ishrâq, illumination.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00189

His reputation for obscurity is illustrated by one of those anecdotes in which Iranian humor gives itself free rein. The story concerns the outward form of the first event awaiting every human being after death: the questioning by the two angels Nâkir and Monkir. They ask the deceased what faith he held and in what God he believed.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00190

So it was with Dâmâd, who naturally could not answer like everyone else. His God? Ostoqos al-ostoqsât: the Element of Elements . . . The two angels are dumbfounded. Nothing like this reply has ever been heard before. What are they to do? They take the matter to the Lord God, who answers them kindly: “Yes, I know. All his life he said things of that sort, which even I could never understand.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00191
“But he is an upright, harmless man. He deserves to enter paradise.”
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00192

What, then, really accounts for the obscure covering in which this thought is wrapped? We must certainly not regard it as a weakness in a mind unable to master its own ideas or find their proper expression. Rather, we should see it as a form of protection—protection from the difficulties and harassment that none of our philosophers, or their students, entirely escaped. This is beautifully illustrated by another anecdote, this time a dream, which contains a wise lesson. After his master’s death, Mollâ Sadrâ sees him in a dream and asks: “Why do people condemn me as an unbeliever (takfîr) when they did not condemn you, even though my doctrines do not differ from yours?”
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00193

Mîr Dâmâd replies: “Because I presented philosophical questions in such a way that the jurists and official theologians could make nothing of them. No one but the sages versed in divine wisdom (ahl-e hikmat) could understand them. You, however, do the opposite. You explain philosophical questions so clearly that any ordinary schoolmaster who happens upon your books can grasp what is at stake. That is why they pronounce you an unbeliever, whereas they could do nothing against me.”
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00194

Should we see a triumph of this “discipline of secrecy,” so rigorously observed by Mîr Dâmâd, in the attitude toward him of the great theologian Majlisî—an attitude that appears paradoxical at first sight? Let me say at once that I am not sure.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00195

But the case is so instructive from another point of view that it is worth recalling. Our evocation of spiritual Isfahan would be incomplete without at least a passing reminder of the paradoxical position of Shiite spiritual thinkers that we examined at the beginning of this work (Book I, Chapter III).
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00196

Mohammad Bâqir Majlisî (d. 1111/1699–1700) is the great theologian of what we may call, though the term is not entirely appropriate, the outward or exoteric Shiite “orthodoxy.” He was an opponent of the Sufis. His aversion to them was so great that he felt compelled to defend the posthumous reputation of his own father, himself an eminent theologian, Mohammad Taqî Majlisî (d. 1070/1659–1660), by emphatically denying that he had ever felt the attraction to Sufism that, in fact, he seems very much to have felt.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00197

Whatever position we take, we cannot withhold our admiration or gratitude for Majlisî’s prodigious labor in organizing Shiite theology. Besides the many books he published in Persian, some kind of research office—an organization whose details are unknown to us—enabled him to produce an immense work: the twenty-six folio volumes of his theological encyclopedia, the Ocean of Lights (Bihâr al-Anwâr).
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00198

But there is more. It was with a certain delighted astonishment that I discovered, amid the dense pages of this encyclopedia, a long account of Mîr Dâmâd written by Majlisî himself. Nothing could be more respectful than its lavish words of praise. Not only does Majlisî quote a beautiful letter from Mîr Dâmâd to his friend Shaykh Bahâ'oddîn 'Âmilî; he even reproduces in full the Risâlat al-Khal'îya, the ecstatic confession translated later in this chapter (§ 3). He introduces it with these simple words: “Among the extraordinary treatises of Mîr Dâmâd, this epistle is evidence of the godlikeness (ta'alloh) of his inmost consciousness. It shows how holy his life was, and what form that life took.”
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00199
Thus the same theologian who was a resolute opponent of the Sufis pays tribute to Mîr Dâmâd the ecstatic mystic.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00200

One might be tempted to find an unintended comedy in this tribute, were the subject not so serious. Had Mîr Dâmâd really succeeded, as he told Mollâ Sadrâ in the dream, in enclosing his actual thought within a web so impenetrable to an outwardly minded theologian that the latter noticed nothing? Had his obscurity deceived Majlisî? That reading would be rather simplistic.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00201

Majlisî’s attitude, despite his opposition to Sufism, is more complex than it first appears. Otherwise, how could he have reproduced, without acknowledgment and as though it were his own, an entire page of Mollâ Sadrâ Shîrâzî in his commentary on Kolaynî’s Kâfî? Besides, the ecstatic confession that Majlisî copied and expressly attributed to Mîr Dâmâd says what it means. Its style is difficult, but it is not written in a deliberately closed or cryptic language.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00202

We also find that, in praising Mîr Dâmâd and discussing this account, Majlisî uses the word ta'alloh. As we know (see Book II, Chapter II), this is a key term among our mystical theosophers, particularly in the vocabulary of the Ishrâqîyûn. It denotes the sacred, reverential devotion through which the Illuminationists aspire to the apotheosis—the becoming godlike—contemplated by the Neoplatonic commentators on the Chaldean Oracles. If Majlisî praises Mîr Dâmâd in these terms, then the horizon open to him in practice was higher and wider than that of a merely literal, outward religion.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00203

The study of religious experience must proceed with the utmost delicacy here, uncovering what lies hidden (bâtin) beneath what is apparent (zâhir). At that deeper level, some oppositions that seem insurmountable on the outward level resolve themselves. It is especially important here to keep in mind a distinction reflected in ordinary Iranian theological usage: that between tasawwof and 'irfân, between Sufism in the strict sense and mystical gnosis, or inward spiritual knowledge.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00204

Majlisî’s reservations about the first are shared by some of the greatest Shiite spiritual masters and mystics. Their criticism is essentially directed at a particular kind of Sufism—the very kind against which Mollâ Sadrâ, who could himself so easily be mistaken for a Sufi, wrote an entire treatise. We have already suggested the reasons: the organization of the Sufi orders (tarîqat), the authority of the shaykh, certain interpretations of monistic metaphysics that did little to encourage moral reform, and certain practices, among other things. These spiritual masters would therefore not accept without qualification Haydar Âmolî’s paradoxical statement that Sufism is true Shiism.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00205

But replace the word Sufism with 'irfân, and one finds broad agreement among all the 'orafâ, those devoted to mystical knowledge. A significant difference is thus concealed beneath a question of vocabulary. In the West, it has become customary simply to equate Islamic mysticism with Sufism. No doubt that is true of Sunnism, where a spiritual seeker who wishes to go beyond the literal forms of religion must “enter Sufism.” It is not true in quite the same way of Shiism, where a believer need only follow the teaching of the holy Imams to its fullest extent to “enter 'irfân.” This is the kind of Shiite spiritual thinker exemplified so perfectly by Mîr Dâmâd and those who came after him. A few details of his life and spiritual descendants will help us see it more clearly.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00206

Both Mîr Dâmâd’s family origins and his spiritual lineage, together with the education he received from an early age, place him within the circle of the great families representing Shiism. Mîr Mohammad Bâqir ibn Shamsoddîn Mohammad Dâmâd Fendereskî Astarâbâdî was born in Astarâbâd in the second half of the tenth Islamic century; his biographers do not allow us to establish the exact year. The name Dâmâd, by which he is usually known, means “son-in-law” in Persian.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00207

Strictly speaking, it had been his father’s nickname, and a pious story explains its origin. His father, Shamsoddîn Mohammad, had been a pupil of Shaykh Nûroddîn 'Alî ibn 'Abd al-'Alî Karakî (d. 945/1538–1539), one of the greatest Imamite scholars. His exceptional learning had earned this mojtahid, a scholar qualified to exercise independent legal judgment, the title Mohaqqiq Thânî, “the Second Investigator”.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00208

Khwânsârî judged that, since Nasîroddîn Tûsî, no scholar had done more than this shaykh to advance Imamite learning. He had studied in Syria, Egypt, and Iraq, and came to Persia under Shah Tahmasp (d. 984/1576), acquiring enormous influence in Isfahan as Shaykh al-Islâm. One night, our Second Investigator dreamed that the First Imam appeared to him and instructed him to give his daughter in marriage to his pupil Shamsoddîn. From their marriage, the Imam said, would be born a child who would inherit the knowledge of the prophets and the holy Imams.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00209

Thus Shamsoddîn became the Dâmâd, the son-in-law of his shaykh. Known by that name, he passed it on to his son, whose life may indeed be said to have fulfilled the lofty destiny announced before his birth.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00210

Mîr Dâmâd studied at Tûs (Mashhad). He came to Isfahan during the reign of Shah 'Abbâs I (996–1038/1588–1629), and from the death of Shah Mohammad (1004/1595–1596) onward, he lived there, wholly devoted to his scholarship and teaching. He belonged to the circle of Shah 'Abbâs, who regarded him with great respect and even a measure of fear, such was his influence. Later he was also among the intimates of Shah Safî (1038–1052 AH).
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00211

All his biographers mention his close and lasting friendship with his great contemporary, the celebrated Shaykh Bahâ'oddîn 'Âmilî (Shaykh-e Bahâ'î), another pillar of Shiite scholarship. He died and was buried in the Holy Land, at Najaf, in 1041/1631–1632. Majlisî tells us that the last words Mîr Dâmâd murmured before dying were those of the Quranic verse: “O soul at peace, return to your Lord, well pleased and pleasing to Him” (89:27–28).
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00212

It would be premature to give a complete list of his works here. The Kitâb al-Ofq al-Mobîn (“Book of the Supreme Horizon,” on being, time, and eternity), the Kitâb Taqwîm al-Imân (“Book of the Rectification of Faith”), the Kitâb al-Sîrat al-Mostaqîm (“Book of the Straight Path”), and the Kitâb al-Qabasât (“Book of Burning Embers,” to which we shall return) were commented upon by his immediate pupils and by later scholars.
